newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Hong Kong assured of freedom under Chinese rule.
newsitem.headline: Hong Kong assured of freedom under Chinese rule.

text.p: Hong Kong entered its final hours as a British colony on Monday with an emotional farewell for Governor Chris Patten and assurances that freedom would survive under Chinese rule.
Chinese President Jiang Zemin, preparing to fly in to receive the territory back from Britain after 156 years on the stroke of midnight (1600 GMT), pledged to uphold human rights and freedom.
Tung Chee-hwa, set to assume power as chief executive of China's special administrative region, promised popular elections for a new legislature within a year.

Symbolising the beginning of the end of colonial rule, Patten left his official residence for the final time barely six hours before the handover after a solemn ceremony under a steady tropical downpour against the background of wailing bagpipes.

Chinese and British staff members wiped tears from their eyes as Patten, the last governor of a major British colony, shook hands and exchanged words with each of them and left to the strains of "Auld Lang Syne".

British Prime Minister Tony Blair, joining a host of world figures gathered for handover celebrations, said he was eager to build a strong and stable relationship with China -- but said Beijing must keep its freedom promises.
After touching down in the rainswept, overcast city -- the last major British colony -- he was asked what message he would deliver in talks with Jiang before the handover ceremony.

"What is absolutely essential is that there are two pillars, foundations of our relationship for the future. The first is adherence to the joint declaration, the agreement between Britain and China that guarantees the future prosperity and freedom of Hong Kong," he said.
"Second is our desire to build a strong and stable relationship with China for the future, which is both in the interests of the people of Hong Kong as well as the people of the United Kingdom."

Shortly afterwards, thousands of Hong Kong Chinese chanting "Tony, we love you" gave Blair and departing Governor Chris Patten a tumultuous reception on a walkabout in one of Hong Kong's palatial shopping malls.
A similar message of affection was given at the same time to thousands of Chinese troops massing on the border before marching into their reclaimed land.
An advance party of 500 was to arrive later on Monday to help prepare the way for a massive second wave of 4,000, accompanied by armour, ships and helicopters, at dawn on Tuesday.

"You must love the people of Hong Kong... and with your actual deeds win the support and love of the Hong Kong people," China's top army officer, General Liu Huaqing, told the People's Liberation Army as it mustered in Shenzhen a few minutes from the colonial frontier.

He reminded the soldiers that Hong Kong would enjoy autonomy under the unique "one country, two systems" formula designed to help the embrace of communist China and rampantly capitalist Hong Kong for the next 50 years.

U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright and British Foreign Secretary Robin Cook on Monday expressed confidence that Hong Kong could maintain its place as a freewheeling economic powerhouse if China stuck to the terms of the 1984 Sino-British Joint Declaration which settled the colony's fate.
Standing beside Cook alongside the royal yacht Britannia, Albright expressed "our expectation that China will keep its word and maintain Hong Kong's autonomy and way of life for decades to come."
Both ministers repeated concerns at the swift and blunt projection of Chinese military power with the arrival of thousands of troops and armour at daybreak on Tuesday.
Hong Kong democrats still have nightmares over the PLA's crushing of democratic dissent in Beijing's Tiananmen Square in 1989.
Veteran democrat Martin Lee told reporters on Monday it was not the timing of the garrisoning of Hong Kong that grated but the manner of it.
"It should be much more low key, instead of invading Hong Kong," he said.

But as a celebratory mood overtook Hong Kong, politicians were trying to put aside longstanding differences which have bedevilled relations between London and Beijing throughout the 90s since Patten introduced democratic reforms.
Cook said Hong Kong would be central to a new Sino-British relationship -- "potentially a bridge, not a barrier..."
The mainly-Chinese 6.4 million population shares a mixed undercurrent of emotions -- elation at returning to the Chinese motherland and concern over future freedoms.
For China itself, it is the end of a century and a half of humiliation from conquest.

Dragon dances, the skirl of bagpipes, massive firework displays and marching bands were the order of the day in Hong Kong as the British bade an emotional farewell and the Chinese swung into party mood.
Beijing streets were festooned with banners proclaiming "Wash away 100 years of national shame". A blimp high over the city declared: "Celebrate the return of Hong Kong".
